new_statements.quote: In Atayal dialects, stress falls on the final or penultimate syllable, depending on the individual dialect as well as individual speaker. It may occasionally vary from item to item. [same page, on Sediq:] All Sediq dialects share the same vowel-deletion rule before stress, which generally falls on the penultimate syllable. In fact, vowel-deletion or weakening in the unstressed syllables is a common phonological feature in the entire Atayalic group except for a few conservative dialects, such as Mayrinax and Matabalay.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on the final or the penultimate syllable; which one depends on the dialect and on the individual speaker, and occasionally on the lexical item. No single fixed position is given for Atayal as a whole. Sediq (a different language) is described as generally penultimate. Unstressed vowels before the stress reduce to schwa in nearly all dialects.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Pre-stress vowels are said to reduce to schwa (except in Toŋan and Maspazi'); a vowel from the infix -in- is retained in the syllable before the main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Variation by dialect, by speaker, and occasionally by item; conservative dialects Mayrinax and Matabalay do not show pre-stress vowel weakening. Footnote 3 (p. 236) on Yang 1976: 'All pretonic vowels before penult are phonetic rather than phonemic'.
new_statements.identity_note: Rau 1992 describes Squliq Atayal as spoken in Wulai (Taipei); most earlier descriptions are of the Gogan dialect of Squliq. Li 1981 covers the whole Atayalic group: Squliq (Pyasan), the C'uli' dialects Maspazi', Skikun, Mnawyan, Mayrinax, Matabalay, Palŋawan, and the Sediq dialects Toŋan, Toda, Truwan, Inago; its penultimate-stress statement is about Sediq, not Atayal. Li 1980 (partially opened) uses a Pyasan-dialect Squliq informant from Tsejen, Fuhsing county, plus Maspazi' for C'uli'.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records fixed final stress; Rau's Wulai Squliq has two stem classes, penultimate (long-vowel/final-schwa stems) versus final (short-vowel stems), with the root's pattern preserved under affixation. Final stress is only one class, not the general rule. The listed hdl.handle.net link resolves to pure.mpg. 9500846), i.e. the same document as work 4; the '2001' in the citation is the UMI reissue date.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penult or the final syllable. Rau ties the choice to vowel length: stems with a long penultimate vowel (pa:qut) have penultimate stress, stems with short vowels (tehuk) have final stress; a word whose final syllable has schwa always stresses the penult. The pattern is stable under affixation (root-stressed: pqútun, thkán), and all vowels before the penult reduce to schwa. Note Rau states the length is posited from the stress ('Roots which have a penultimate stress are analyzed here to contain a long vowel'), so for prediction the contrast is effectively lexical (two stem classes) with root-preserving stress; conclusion p. 196: 'It is found that stress characterizes this language: the affixed form has the same stress pattern as the root.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; pre-penult vowels reduce to schwa (§2.4.1), which argues against secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-schwa words always penultimate; the infix -in- occasionally resists reduction in the antepenult; long-vowel stems keep the penult unreduced when suffixed while short-vowel stems reduce the penult; some stems lose a whole syllable when suffixed (§2.4.2).

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Squliq Atayal (Pyasan dialect, the basis of sec. 2), word stress normally falls on the final syllable; the penultimate vowel is phonetically long; vowels before the penult are deleted/reduced to a predictable [ə] that never bears stress; under suffixation the stress shifts onto the suffix (i.e. stays word-final), which drives the vowel deletions of sec. 2.4.6-2.4.7. No separate stress statement is made for the C?uli? dialects (Maspazi?, Skikun, Mayrinax, etc.); the introduction lists 'vowel-deletion before stress' as a drift shared across the Atayalic group.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned; only the phonetic lengthening of the penultimate vowel ([βu:kíl], [pi:máʔ]) is noted
new_statements.exceptions: only the hedge 'normally'; no lexical or dialectal exceptions to final stress are listed; sec. 3 gives no stress statement for the C?uli? dialects (it notes only that vowels before the penult are preserved in C?uli?/Mayrinax and lost in Squliq/Skikun/Mnawyan, pp. 377, 388)
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1980 treats Squliq (represented by the Pyasan dialect, informant from Tse-jen village, Fu-hsing, Taoyuan) and C?uli? dialects Maspazi?, Skikun, Mayrinax, Matabalay, Sakuxan and Palngawan (per the abstract and p. 349); the stress section 2.2 belongs to the Squliq phonology chapter.

readall_conflicts: The catalog (StressTyp2) records Atayal as fixed final stress. Neither open source that could be read supports a fixed: final syllable rule as stated. Rau 1992 (Squliq of Wulai) gives two stem classes: penultimate stress in stems with a long penultimate vowel or a final schwa, final stress in short-vowel stems, with the root's pattern kept under affixation (páqut/pqútun vs. tehúk/thkán); she herself notes the length is inferred from the stress, so the split is in practice lexical. Li 1981 (pan-Atayalic survey) says stress is final or penultimate depending on the dialect and the individual speaker, occasionally varying by item, and gives Sediq (a different language) as generally penultimate. Rau and Li are compatible with each other (both final-or-penult), but both disagree with a single fixed final position; the catalog's rule may reflect the Squliq speakers or sources (e.g. Egerod) for whom final stress predominates. Li 1980, whose §2.2 'Vowels and Stress' would be the most direct Squliq statement, could not be obtained (host unreachable, Internet Archive copy truncated). The catalog's StressTyp2-derived record has Atayal as fixed word-final stress. Rau 1992 (p. Li 1981 (BIHP 52(2), p. 239; held by the project from the verification, not a listed work here) independently says that in Atayal dialects 'stress falls on the final or penultimate syllable, depending on the individual dialect as well as individual speaker' and 'may occasionally vary from item to item', which sides…
